R060-01.notes: Paragraphs 1-2 argue the charges work, and the last paragraph says benefits 'are easier to see once people have lived with it.' D covers only one detail. C contradicts 'not that a price solves every transportation problem.' B: the passage never ranks London against Stockholm.

flags.note: The stem says 'a majority of Stockholm residents voted,' but the passage says 'a majority of voters in the city.' Those are different groups, and Passage B makes exactly this point (voters are not always the people who bear the costs). Rewording the stem to 'a majority of voters in Stockholm' would fix it.

R060-02.notes: The vote reversed the opposition residents showed before the trial, which supports the claim that benefits become clearer with experience. A is the reverse of the passage ('most residents opposed'). D mixes up cause and effect. B overreaches.

R060-03.notes: Nearly a word-for-word lift from the passage. A (rerouting) is the trap that sounds plausible. This is a normal detail item.

R060-04.notes: The example illustrates 'not the same burden for everyone.' C (exempting aides) goes beyond the passage. D contradicts 'No one seriously disputes that a congestion charge can cut traffic.'

R060-05.notes: Matches 'fairness depends on what a city does with the money and on what alternatives it offers.' A contradicts 'does not mean that charges are a mistake.' B is the 'neutral' view the author rejects. C contradicts the author's doubts about referendums.

flags.note: Distractors B, C and D (electrical, wartime, color senses) clearly have nothing to do with traffic policy, so a student can pick A without reading the context. A stronger item would use near-miss senses such as 'impartial/unbiased in opinion' or 'having no effect,' so that the 'same fee for everyone' context actually decides the answer.

R060-06.notes: The context is 'everyone pays the same fee.' The answer is right, but the distractors are weak.

R060-07.notes: This is the third paragraph of Passage B in other words. C is the best trap ('voters are not always the ones who bear costs'), but B never calls the vote invalid. D contradicts B's first sentence. A is the reverse of B's view.

R060-08.notes: A: trips shifted, combined, or made by bus. B: 'No one seriously disputes that a congestion charge can cut traffic,' which implies travel behavior changes. A is rejected by B. Passage A never weighs revenue (B), and B's author doubts referendums (D). C is a modest inference for B, but none of the other options is defensible.

R060-09.notes: The sentence contrasts how revenue is used. C contradicts 'identical.' A and D are not in the passage.

R060-10.notes: B is about burdens and fairness. B, C and D are all Passage A's emphasis or are things Passage B grants without argument.
